To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the growth-based structural model for VLSI circuit interconnection is a plausible alternative to the power-law scaling phenomena that currently dominate VLSI interconnection estimation and that the growth-based model is equally plausible, yet different, from the Rent model.
(1) VLSI circuits exhibit a power-law distribution of fanout, crossing edges and terminals.

(1) a random growth model that assumes that each new cell is connected to a random existing cell is able to predict the number of fanout edges in a design, (2) the number of crossing edges is well predicted by a random growth model with a random number of connections per cell, and (3) a random growth-based model with a random terminal distribution can accurately predict the number of terminals.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the power-law scaling phenomena that have been used to model VLSI circuit structure are not universal and that alternative power-law phenomena exist.
the power-law scaling phenomena that have formed the foundation of interconnect estimation for decades may be replaced with a new class of models.
the Rent's rule is not the only possible model that can be used to describe the structural properties of VLSI circuits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our models can explain the same phenomena as Rent's rule, but with a different interpretation of the parameters.
the power-law scaling phenomena in VLSIs is not as well understood and as universal as previously thought.
the structural models for VSI circuits are not unique and the Rent's rule may not be the only possible scaling model for interconnects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the power-law scaling phenomena in VLSIs are not unique and that there are other power-law models that are equally plausible.
the power-law scaling phenomenon that underpins VLSI interconnection estimation is not unique.
the scaling of VLSI circuits may not necessarily be governed by Rent's law and that the scaling of the interconnect structure may be more complex than previously thought.
